question: Where and when does Ezekiel receive his first vision, and what does the text say about his situation and that of the people?
The word דְּמוּת (demut, “likeness”) is repeated throughout the vision, up to “the likeness of the glory of the LORD”: why does the prophet describe what he sees so cautiously?
What can the wheels that move in every direction, guided by the spirit, communicate to exiles far from the temple in Jerusalem?
Before the glory of the LORD, Ezekiel falls on his face: what place does reverence have in the way you approach God?
To whom is Ezekiel sent, and how are these people described?
The word מְרִי (meri, “rebellion”) appears in “rebellious house” several times: what contrast does God draw between the people's rebellion and what He expects of the prophet in verse 8?
What does it mean that the mission has value “whether they listen or refuse to listen,” and how does this change the measure of the prophet's success?
God tells Ezekiel “do not be afraid of them” even among briers and scorpions: in what situation do you need to speak the truth despite fear of the reaction?
What happens when Ezekiel eats the scroll, and what contrast is there between its taste and the contents described in chapter 2?
The verb צָפָה (tsafah, “watch”) defines Ezekiel as a watchman for the house of Israel: what responsibilities do verses 17 to 21 assign to this watchman?
Why does God shut Ezekiel inside his house and leave him mute, opening his mouth only when He has something to say?
Ezekiel sits stunned among the exiles for seven days before speaking: what value is there in being with those who suffer before saying any word?
What symbolic actions must Ezekiel perform with the brick, the iron plate and the positions of his body?
The word עָוֺן (‘avon, “iniquity, guilt”) appears in the command for the prophet to “bear” the iniquity of Israel and Judah: what does it mean for a prophet to carry the people's guilt this way?
What do the measured bread and rationed water announce about the future of Jerusalem, and why does Ezekiel protest in verse 14?
God heeds Ezekiel's protest and changes the instruction: what does this dialogue show about speaking honestly with God?
What does Ezekiel do with his hair and beard, and what happens to each part?
The word שְׁלִישִׁי (shelishi, “third part”) organizes the sign and its explanation: how do verses 2 and 12 correspond to each other?
Why is Jerusalem, set “in the center of the nations,” judged so severely, according to verses 5 to 9?
A few strands are kept in the fold of the garment: what does this small gesture suggest to you in the middle of a chapter of judgment?
To whom is this prophecy addressed, and what places of worship does it announce will be destroyed?
The word גִּלּוּל (gilul, “idol”) appears several times in the chapter; many scholars link it to a root that recalls dung: what does the use of this term reveal about the prophet's view?
What role does the remnant that escapes have, and what does it mean that they will remember God and “loathe themselves”?
God says He was crushed by their “adulterous hearts”: what changes in you when you think that your turning away affects God?
What words and phrases are repeated in the announcement of verses 2 to 9, and what effect does this repetition produce?
The word קֵץ (qets, “end”) sounds several times at the beginning of the chapter: what did it mean for those still living in the land of Israel to hear that “the end has come”?
Why can silver and gold not deliver the people “in the day of the LORD's wrath,” and how did they become the “stumbling block” of their iniquity?
The people seek peace, vision and counsel when it is already too late: what counsel have you put off seeking until a crisis arrives?
What four scenes of abomination does Ezekiel see in the temple, and who takes part in each one?

The word תּוֹעֵבַה (to‘evah, “abomination”) grows from scene to scene with the refrain “greater abominations”: what kind of practices does it name here, and why do they drive God away from the sanctuary?
What does the elders' saying “The LORD does not see us; the LORD has forsaken the land” reveal, and how does it explain what they did in secret?
The elders do in the dark what they would not do in public: what difference is there between your life “in the shrines” and the one others see?
Who are the characters who appear in this chapter, and what task does the man clothed in linen receive?

The mark placed on the forehead is תָּו (tav), the name of the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet, which in the old script was shaped like a cross or an X: who receives this sign, and what does it indicate about these people?
Why must the judgment begin “at My sanctuary,” and how does this idea appear elsewhere in the Bible?
Those marked are the ones who “sigh and groan” over the abominations of the city: what saddens you in the place where you live, and what do you do with that sadness?
What does the man clothed in linen do with the burning coals, and where is the glory of the LORD at this moment?
The word כְּרוּב (kerub, “cherub”) dominates the chapter: how does Ezekiel realize that the beings of this vision are the same as those at the Chebar River?
What does it mean that the glory of the LORD leaves the threshold of the house and stops at the east gate, and what effect would this have on those who trusted in the temple?
The same glory that filled the house is about to leave it: what does this scene say to you about trusting in places and rituals without a living relationship with God?
Who are the twenty-five men at the east gate, and what does the saying “this city is the cauldron, and we are the meat” mean?
How does God answer the inhabitants of Jerusalem who despised the exiles, and what does it mean that He will be “a sanctuary” for them in a foreign land?
Verse 19 sets a “heart of stone” against a “heart of flesh,” using בָּשָׂר (basar, “flesh”): what does this exchange promise, and how does it relate to the “new spirit”?
What area of your life seems hardened like stone and needs this transformation God promises?
What actions must Ezekiel perform with the baggage, the wall and his covered face, and who must watch all of this?
The word מוֹפֵת (mofet, “sign”) defines the prophet himself: what does it mean for Ezekiel's life to become a sign for the people?
What sayings were going around about the prophets' visions, and how does God answer them in verses 21 to 28?
The people thought the word was “for the distant future”: what warnings do you treat as something for later?
